hints: Think about the two opposite forces at the capillary wall: blood (hydrostatic) pressure pushing fluid out, and plasma proteins pulling water back in.
Ask yourself, what happens to osmosis back into the blood if there are fewer plasma proteins to lower the water potential of the blood?
walkthrough:
**Recall how tissue fluid is made and removed**

Think of the capillary as leaky. High blood pressure at the arteriole end pushes water and small solutes out to form tissue fluid.

Further along, blood pressure falls, so water is drawn back into the blood by osmosis.

**Remember the role of plasma proteins**

Plasma proteins are too large to leave the capillary. They give blood plasma a lower (more negative) water potential than tissue fluid.

So water moves from tissue fluid (higher water potential) to blood plasma (lower water potential) by osmosis. This reabsorbs fluid and prevents build up.

**Apply this to oedema**

If plasma protein concentration is lower than normal, the water potential of the blood is higher (less negative) than normal.

Less water is reabsorbed by osmosis, so more fluid is left behind around the cells. That accumulation is oedema.

options.A: Lower blood pressure would push less fluid out of the capillary, so less tissue fluid would form, not more.
options.B: Lower plasma protein raises the water potential of blood, so less water moves back in by osmosis and excess tissue fluid accumulates.
options.C: Higher plasma protein would lower blood water potential even more, so more water would be reabsorbed and tissue fluid would decrease.
options.D: Lower tissue fluid protein would raise tissue fluid water potential, increasing the gradient for osmosis back into the blood, so tissue fluid would decrease.
